s1b1.text: Every team has principles. They hang on a wall, or sit in a slide deck. And then Monday starts.

s1b2.text: So what do principles look like in real work? Not on a slide, but in a repository?

s1b3.text: Meet Tip again. Tip is a small iceberg, and today Tip shows you four of our principles, using one real project.

s1b4.text: The Iceberg Data Platform: an open data platform that I build together with an AI agent.

s1b5.text: Four principles. Four places to look.

s2b1.text: Principle one: AI native. AI operates. You architect.

s2b2.text: You put AI to work on what it's good at: code, tests, analysis and first drafts. You stay accountable for the framing, the trade-offs, and everything that goes live.

s2b3.text: In the platform, an AI agent writes most of the code, the tests and the first drafts of the designs.

s2b4.text: But the real questions come back to a person. Kubernetes now, or only a design? A two-hour token, or a setting? Each answer is a human call.

s2b5.text: And nothing goes live on the agent's word. A release only ships when a person tags it, and only after the full test run passes.

s3b1.text: Principle two: everything as code. If it matters, it lives in the repo.

s3b2.text: Docs, deployments and architecture are versioned, reviewed and diffable. Nothing important lives in a wiki page, a console click, or somebody's head.

s3b3.text: In the platform, the docs sit next to the code. The installer, the deployment and the release pipeline are files in the same repository.

s3b4.text: Even the contracts between the parts are files. If the code and its contract drift apart, a test fails.

s3b5.text: The agent's instructions live there too, in an agents file and a set of skills. And so does this video: its script, its sources and its music are code.

s4b1.text: Principle three: own the decision. Decide in the open. Own the outcome.

s4b2.text: Write down why, not just what. Build it, and run it. And design for composability and portability, so today's choice never becomes tomorrow's cage.

s4b3.text: Big choices in the platform get a decision record: what we chose, what we didn't choose, and why.

s4b4.text: For example, pipeline runs get no internet, on purpose. The record says why, so nobody has to guess later.

s4b5.text: We run what we build: an infrastructure page shows the health of every container, extensions included.

s4b6.text: And the parts talk through open standards: Iceberg tables, S3 storage, OpenID Connect for sign-in, and MCP for agents. So one part can be replaced without touching the others.

s5b1.text: Principle four: stay relevant. The market moves. So do we.

s5b2.text: Own the capability roadmap, not the tool roadmap. Every tool we run has a successor, and an exit date we set ourselves.

s5b3.text: The platform is a map of capabilities: a catalog, storage, sign-in, an engine, and a place to work. Each one is filled by a tool, and each tool can be swapped.

s5b4.text: Bots check the dependencies every week. And before this release, an agent swept the repository for anything that had gone stale. Thirteen releases in just over three weeks.

s5b5.text: Design records name the successor before it's needed: pipeline runs use Docker today, and a Kubernetes design is ready for later.

s5b6.text: And the contract between the parts has a written policy: from version one, an old version keeps running next to the new one for at least a release. We set the exit date.

s6b1.text: Four principles. AI operates, you architect. If it matters, it's in the repo. Decide in the open. And keep moving.

s6b2.text: None of them needs a poster to be true. Each one shows up in a file, a test, or a decision you can read.

s6b3.text: So next Monday, open your repository and ask: where can someone see our principles at work?

s6b4.text: If the answer is everywhere, they're under the water, holding everything up.
